title: Adopting a structured logging library over ad-hoc console.log
notes: Clean architecture decision session choosing a structured logging library, with reasoning about queryability and log levels.

turns.text: Our logs are just scattered console.log() calls with no consistent format. It's painful to search production logs when something breaks. Should we adopt a real logging library?

Yes, I'd recommend pino — it emits structured JSON logs by default, which makes them queryable in whatever log aggregator we're using, and it's one of the fastest Node logging libraries so it won't add meaningful overhead on hot paths.
How's that different from just JSON.stringify-ing our console.log calls?

Mainly log levels and context propagation — pino gives us debug/info/warn/error levels we can filter by per-environment, and child loggers that carry request-scoped context (like requestId) automatically into every log line without threading it through manually.

It's incremental-friendly — we can wrap it so existing console.log call sites keep working during migration, then replace them file-by-file with logger.info/error calls that include structured fields. No need for a big-bang rewrite.
Adding pino as the logging library, with a request-scoped child logger attaching requestId to every log line, and log level configurable per environment via LOG_LEVEL.
